title: How much of Earth is actually water?

narration.heading: Planet Ocean
narration.text: From space, our planet looks like it's made almost entirely of water.

narration.heading: 71% blue
narration.text: Oceans cover about seventy-one percent of the surface. Nearly three quarters of everything you can see.

narration.heading: The Pacific
narration.text: The Pacific alone covers more than thirty percent of the planet. It's bigger than all the continents put together.

narration.heading: How deep?
narration.text: And it's deep. The ocean averages almost four kilometres down, and the Challenger Deep plunges nearly eleven.

narration.heading: Too salty
narration.text: But you can't drink it. Ninety-six and a half percent of all Earth's water sits in the salty oceans.

narration.heading: Fresh water
narration.text: Only two and a half percent is fresh. And most of that is frozen solid in glaciers and ice sheets.

narration.heading: One lake
narration.text: Meanwhile one lake in Siberia, Baikal, holds a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on the planet.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: Now pour every drop on Earth into a single ball. It would be only about fourteen hundred kilometres wide.

narration.heading: Your guess?
narration.text: A blue planet with surprisingly little water. So how much of it could you actually drink? Guess below.

titles: What if you poured all of Earth's water into one ball?
Earth is 71% ocean, but has surprisingly little water
youtube.description: A spin around the globe from the Pacific to Lake Baikal, ending with every drop of Earth's water squeezed into a single ball.

sources.claim: About 71% of Earth's surface is ocean; 96.5% of Earth's water is in the oceans; 2.5% is fresh water, 68.7% of it in glaciers
The Pacific covers more than 30% of Earth's surface and is larger than all the continents combined
Average ocean depth about 3,682 m; Challenger Deep about 10,935 m
Lake Baikal contains 20% of the world's total unfrozen fresh water
All the water on Earth would form a sphere about 860 miles (about 1,385 km) across
